utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP17, can you mark that with number 13?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17
utterances.text: Yes. Mortars which were used from Sokolje too, that is number 14, from Dobrinja, so those would be the positions. Those are the ones that I can remember. That's where the mortar nests were.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP17, to sum up you mentioned heavy weapons, you mentioned tanks, guns, multiple rocket launchers, you mentioned mortars, you mentioned the calibres. Can you tell us whether you personally know about any other heavy weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17
utterances.text: Well, there were anti-aircraft machine-guns, 12.7 millimetre so-called Brownings. I said that they had a lot of Osas and a lot of Zoljas rocket launchers and hand held rocket launchers.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP17, do you personally know how the BH Army armed itself? Were you yourself in a position to see the weapons that the BH Army had?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17
utterances.text: Yes. I could -- I had the opportunity of seeing the weapons and the ammunition. So it was easy for my to distinguish ammunition from European countries, from ammunition from Argentina since they had such markings, and there was ammunition from Eastern Europe -- eastern Germany, correction. And as far as rifles are concerned they also had so-called M-16 American rifles, they had quite a few Kalashnikov and that was also the time I saw before the conflict broke out on the 1st of March, a month or and before I saw Hungarian Kalashnikovs at the barricades. That's the first time I saw them. And then I asked the Muslims what sort of weapons are they, and they said that they were Hungarian Kalashnikovs.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. DP17. When you say that you were -- you personally had the opportunity of seeing ammunitions, et cetera, while you were present in that area and during the conflict, did you have the opportunity of seeing those weapons in -- at a certain time and at a certain location?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17
utterances.text: Well, yes. In Ilidza itself the Military Police stopped convoys on several occasions, convoys that were escorting UNPROFOR forces and of course in routine checkups they found ammunition and weapons as well as Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. projectiles, that is to say, mortar shells. And also powder for making shells and rifle launched grenades.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP17, now that you have told us about this, were you personally present, did you see who --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17
utterances.text: Well, yes, I was also personally present there. There was such situations, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my colleague suggests that -- says that there is a mistake in the transcript. If he could clarify this, I think it says "of European production."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What exactly is the line where the problem appears.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Behind, so perhaps you could read the line in which you would like --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. But could the witness take his headphones off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please put them first on. Yes. Do you understand or read any English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You studied psychology but you do not read any English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Russian, as you know was studied a bit in our schools.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please take your headphones off. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, if you -- I will listen to you on the French channel, that perhaps would be the wisest.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Thank you, Mr. President. I think that I heard -- I think that I heard the witness say as far as the production of weapons is concerned, that it concerned Arab countries and not -- Arab companies not European companies. In Serbian language the two words are very similar. Could we just check this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, no loud speaking in B/C/S. It is -- I know it is difficult --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry, and sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you told us about the ammunition --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. It is rather stupid of me to address you when I first asked you to take your earphones off. When you talked about the ammunition and where it was produced, could you please repeat where, according to your experience, the ammunition was produced?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the ammunition had Arab marks and from Argentina and from eastern Germany and also ammunition which was produced in Cojic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for your clarification. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP17, I think you said that you personally had the opportunity of seeing that. Where were you able to see this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17
utterances.text: In the centre of Ilidza itself, in the course of a checkup, a control, we found ammunition for Brownings, those are heavy anti-aircraft machine-guns which are also used when -- against manpower, against the infantry.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP17, I have to interrupt you there. You said that you personally observed that. Can you tell us whether you were personally present and in what kind of vehicles, if you saw this from vehicles?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17
utterances.text: I was personally present in vehicles which were allegedly transporting humanitarian aid to Sarajevo. It is in those vehicles that we found ammunition and medical supplies, if my memory is correct. It was for the army, for the town of Sarajevo, the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Defence has a video cassette that has been disclosed to the Prosecution. It is number 348, number 4. With your permission could we see -- could we watch this video cassette so that the witness could identify --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are we going to just watch or also listen, Ms. Pilipovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we will listen to it too. Defence has prepared a translation and it is two minutes long, the cassette is two minutes long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that the technical booth is prepared to play that video? If you would then first --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A copy of the translation has been --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Provided to the booth?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've provided a copy, Your Honour, but could that part be -- could we remain in closed session for that part because the witness can be seen on the cassette.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, let's do something in a logical sequence. The translators have been provided with the translation you have prepared. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And my colleagues from the Prosecution have been provided with a copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And before we turn into private session, I would first like to hear from Mr. Mundis whether the objection or observation or consent he wants to express should be done in open -- in private session or in open. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, just simply the Prosecution has no objection to the tape being shown.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then we turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. DP17, can you answer this question, you personally, what kind of personal knowledge do you have of such checkups?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17
utterances.text: I have personal knowledge and Obrad Popadic who is a colleague of mine, he found under the containers transported by UNPROFOR, and as far as I remember that was also recorded on videotape and our television broadcast this, and I remember this that the UNPROFOR forces said that they are not responsible for the load, they were only responsible for the safe passage of the convoy. That is what they said on that occasion. And I also remember that Colonel Cojic from the Igman Brigade at the crossing of Kobiljaca found many rifles of American production and ammunition that were in transporters, and there was this attempt of them to cross into Sarajevo so that they would end up in the hands of Muslim fighters.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17
utterances.text: There is more, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP17, I will ask you the following question. When you are speaking about the UNPROFOR, can you tell us whether you had direct opportunity to be present or rather what kind of cooperation with UNPROFOR did you have, you personally, did you have any cooperation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17
utterances.text: Well, personally there was a cooperation on this level, at this post where I was and also on the level of the brigade. Personally not in a sense that there was animosity between us. We respected each other, but obviously there were criticisms when some incidents happened we protested adamantly when these incidents occurred. That was not their mandate to do this and that was something that was done specifically against us.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP17, when you say that you had contacts with members of UNPROFOR, apart from what you've told us, what else did you speak about at meetings with UNPROFOR? What were the important issues for your area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17
utterances.text: Well, the meetings that I attended mostly, among other things, you could see this for yourself, for instance, there was addressing of criticisms and requests and not to have this happen again, and also there was an exchange of information in a sense when shells came from their side and falling across the wider area of Ilidza, which incidents civilians were killed. We also addressed this kind of criticism and protest. And there were other discussions. But this is basically what discussions were about. This is mostly the nature that I -- of these discussions that I mentioned. That would be the essence.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP17, do you personally have knowledge whether in the area of your brigade there were observation posts, UN observation posts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17
utterances.text: There were three observation posts. One was in front of our command, practically right next to the line, that is the line which goes eastwards towards Hrasnica, Sokolovic colony and so on, that is where the UNPROFOR forces were positioned. No, I am sorry. I don't mean forces in general, but there was the French battalion was positioned there. The second observation post was Zetra -- I am sorry time has passed so I can't quite remember. But that was on the line towards a city, towards Stup and that was in the area of responsibility of Muslim forces. And then there was one observation post which was in Nedzarici itself practically on the line, precisely on the line between Dobrinja and Nedzarici. More specifically towards Vojnicko Polje, that was the closest area was Vojnicko Polje. And there was one fourth -- fourth observation post that is as much I can remember was in Energoinvest.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP17, when you listed these observation posts of the UN, can you tell us, you personally, whether you had the opportunity to speak with UN forces member and what did these discussions consist of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17
utterances.text: Yes, we did. Very frequently we were bitter and angry. We addressed this protest from General Galic during truces that were very frequently agreed and signed, but none of these truces were respected by the Muslim forces. And I remember one case when we had several people who were injured and who were killed, and I asked the General, the here present General, I asked, "What should we do? They have killed our people. They are killing our people." And he said: "You should be injured too, but we cannot answer fire because it is truce. These are the rules. We cannot, we must not respond with fire." And that was -- these were the discussions and also requests to the UNPROFOR forces on these posts that I have listed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP17, can you tell us whether you have personal knowledge, if you know, how long did it last that observation post in Nedzarici, what was the period of time that we are talking about? If you know.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17
utterances.text: Well, it was for several months continually, even longer. Well, there were so many facts and so many details, so I cannot be absolutely certain about that. I would rather not speculate.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. DP17 --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17
utterances.text: I am sorry. As far as the observation post in front of the command, I know that it was there almost until the end of the war because it is something that was within my view.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. DP17, can you tell us in the area of Nedzarici, do you know where was the command post, that is, which unit was in the Nedzarici area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17
utterances.text: In the Nedzarici area was the battalion and it later became company. And the command of the battalion again we called it 1st Nedzarici Battalion, and it consisted of the company in the airport locality and the company in Kasindolska Street. And to start with, initially, the command was in the building of the former barracks. It is a ground-floor building. And sometime in 1994 in early 1994 I believe it was moved to Kasindolska Street. This command was moved. Or allow me just a moment -- no, it wasn't in 1994. It was in 1995 that it was moved to Kasindolska Street.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. DP17, can you tell us do you know at the command of the brigade, did you receive reports from your battalions and how did you receive them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17
utterances.text: Reports arrived on daily basis and they were written reports. These reports were compiled regarding all the events that happened throughout the day. And these reports were done also by assistant commander for morale, for logistics, for security and by the battalion commander himself. So such reports came to the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP17, when you say that you received reports at the brigade command, can you tell us whether on the level of the brigade were reports compiled on the level of the brigade and what would enter into those reports and who did they go to? Who were they forwarded to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17
utterances.text: Every day at the end of the day in the hours of the evening following reception of reports from battalions, that is from the entire area of responsibility of the brigade in question, there would be a report compiled that would go to the corps command. And these reports mostly contained the security situation in the brigade, the numbers, that is the strength in the brigade, activity with the brigade, enemy activity, logistics support, the morale in the brigade. These were mostly the issues that were covered in the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence would like to show the witness some documents that were disclosed to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you please assist Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP17, do you recognise this document? Mr. DP17, could you please put the document on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17
utterances.text: I recognise this document and the person who compiled the document and forwarded it, this is the kind of document that were forwarded with the daily report, and we sent it to the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP17, in this report in the left corner, does it say 13th of December 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Below the -- below in the document does it say "daily report"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: And then it says "to the command of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP17, can you read the situation and the activity of the enemy? Is that what it says in the document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17
utterances.text: Situation activity on the enemy, throughout the day to day, the enemy at the time of 1400 hours -- I am sorry -- throughout the day to day at the time of 1400 hours the enemy intensively shelled the wider area of Ilidza while the main targets of the enemy were important strategic facilities as follows: The transformer station at Svrelo Bosna, hospital in Blazuj and civilian facilities in the locality.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. DP17, you told us that these reports were forwarded to the Sarajevo Romanija Corps command every day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17
utterances.text: Yes. These reports with similar contents.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence would like to show the witness DP17 another document. D1313.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP17, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP17, in the left corner on this document do you see -- do we have the date 14th of December 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP17 is it also a daily report?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Under item 1, situation and activity of the enemy, could you please read what it says in the first three lines of this item about the situation and the activity.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17
utterances.text: Yes. "The enemy during the day and during the early evening was not quiet, was not still. On several occasions it could be heard from Mount Igman with artillery firing on a wider area of Ilidza, although the firing wasn't frequent."

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. DP17, this document, do you also recognise the person who compiled this report?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP17, you told us that after the enemy broke the truce you spoke directly to the Corps Commander, General Galic. Can you tell us, you personally, how frequently did you meet or did you have the opportunity between September 1992 and August 1994, how frequently were you able to meet General Galic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17
utterances.text: Well, I met him on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "several occasions" can you tell us how many times is that and where?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17
utterances.text: Well, at least three or four times, considering the post that I had, I was subordinate in the chain of command of the brigade. So three or four times in the corps itself, and some ten times in the brigade when the General came to inspect the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You personally, were you present or were there any meetings at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17
utterances.text: Well, certainly there were official meetings in relation to the security situation in the brigade, activities of the enemy, in relation to the analysis of the logistical support and other military matters that could be on the agenda, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am thinking whether it is time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If this is a suitable moment for you, we will have a break until five minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, I was informed that you wanted to address the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. It might be appropriate for it to be done in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will then turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my colleague will continue with the examination of the witness for the time that remains.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And I will take advantage of this opportunity to say that the Prosecution made a slight error. We didn't have a meeting, this meeting -- a meeting this morning, at least I don't remember such a meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, good day. Could you please answer my questions by saying yes or no, if this is possible, yes, no.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, could you perhaps approach the microphone so or perhaps the usher could assist us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is that all right?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perfect. I think it should be all right for the French booth too. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, I'd like to return to the issue of weapons. And in particular to the issue of -- of mortars that you mentioned. On the map you marked sites where numbers 8, 9, and 10, indicating battery positions. Do you remember doing this; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, could you tell us what the range of these batteries was in terms of the shot?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17
utterances.text: Well, it depended on the calibre and the charge, how forceful the charge was that would be used for the mortar when a shell was being fired. So it -- a 60-millimetre mortar was -- had a range of under 2 kilometres. And then the range would go up to 6 kilometres or more, that would be the range of a 120-millimetre mortar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could you tell us, Witness, from the positions that you have indicated with the numbers 8, 9, and 10, what was the distance as the crow flies, what was the distance separating these batteries from the Alipasino Polje area, roughly speaking?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17
utterances.text: Well, up to about 4 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, do you know whether -- I withdraw that. Witness, do you know what type of mortar, that is to say what calibre, the enemy side had at positions 8, 9, and 10, the positions that you have mentioned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17
utterances.text: 82-millimetres, 60, and 120-millimetres.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, I would like you to focus on the cassette that we saw a minute ago, on the videocassette that we saw a minute ago. I am referring to the lorries that we saw. It is not necessary to refer to names or anything else really. I think we saw a driver. What happened to this driver, can you tell us very briefly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17
utterances.text: All the drivers were returned to their homeland.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: When, and if this is relevant, after what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17
utterances.text: Given that such questions were complex, the corps would deal with these issues. We referred them to the corps and those responsible in the corps, I know from conversations with these persons that after a certain period of time, I don't know how long, they were sent back to their homeland.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, I am going to interrupt you there. If you don't know exactly, if you don't know the answer, then say you don't know the answer and then we will move on to another subject. Thank you. You mentioned an Army Corps. Have you ever heard about the existence of a plan at the level of an Army Corps, the purpose of which would be to eliminate the entire population, the entire Muslim population in Sarajevo; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. That's a leading question. Leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Piletta-Zanin --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, absolutely, Mr. President, but I thought that there was a rule, according to which when a certain point is not contested by the parties one could intervene in a direct manner in order to save time. But I will reformulate that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There would be no dispute between the parties as to the existence of such a plan, then I would like to know in what respect the parties agree on this issue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. DP17, have you knowledge on the policy of the military commanders or political commanders in the Sarajevo area, what they were aiming at?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I never heard about the total elimination of Muslims and I think this is a way of thinking that is inappropriate for Serbs and for commanders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, would you please move to your next subject. We now heard an answer to the question, but let me be quite clear on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Sometimes, and it is not the first time that I draw your attention to that, sometimes by putting the question -- a leading question to the witness, the effect cannot be undone. One of the possible responses of the Chamber could also be that you have to move to your next subject without getting an answer and without the question being reformulated either by the Chamber or yourself. Please proceed on your next subject. The question has been answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Gladly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, a minute ago you spoke about mortars. Did you see mortar impacts during the period that you were involved in the fighting in Sarajevo; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Since you saw them, what was the calibre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17
utterances.text: Well, I saw the impacts caused by shells of all calibres that I have mentioned, that the Muslim side had. If necessary I can tell you which ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. We all remember the four calibres that you mentioned. I am interested in the 120-millimetre calibre. Did you see craters caused by 120-millimetre calibre mortar shells in an asphalt terrain; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you see many such craters; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, to the extent that you saw many such craters caused by 120-millimetre mortar shells in asphalt, what can you tell us about what happens to what we call either the tail-fin or the stabiliser?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17
utterances.text: Mostly I didn't even see this. When it exploded it would disintegrate more or less, or it would fly off into the distance, but I really didn't have the opportunity of seeing the tail-fin near the crater unless the valve, the safety valve would be taken out. And then the shell would be embedded in the asphalt and then you would see the tail, that is to say the tail-fin of the shell.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, if I have -- in order to understand your testimony correctly, in such a situation since you mentioned -- I will reformulate that. Could you please tell us what this sort of safety valve is that you have mentioned and what is the purpose of this valve?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17
utterances.text: Well, all mortar shells have a safety valve. And before using it, before putting the shell into the mortar barrel it has to be removed. So this purpose of the safety valve is to prevent the shell from exploding when it is being handled. Sometimes when people are in a hurry, they would forget to take it out. The shell could fall out of the barrel, it could hit the territory that is being targeted but it wouldn't explode if the safety valve remained in the shell, and then the tail-fin would remain intact, the tail-fin that you mentioned, it would be part of the body of the shell.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. And with regard to your previous testimony, what you testified about a minute ago. When you say "the tail-fin is embedded" you mean in such situation, in situations when the shell doesn't explode; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17
utterances.text: Yes, clearly, clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, I would now like to move on to a different subject and I would like to examine the issue of orders. Did you receive in your combat zone any orders from the military hierarchy regarding, first of all, the use of ammunition; and then secondly, concerning the issue of respecting civilians? Could you answer that question by saying yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you now tell us in a couple of words what the nature of the orders you received was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17
utterances.text: Well, the orders that we received were to save ammunition and only to fire at people bearing weapons, and we relayed these orders to certain soldiers at the lines, to subordinates and soldiers at the lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Did you yourself relay these orders; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Could you tell us on how many occasions and in what circumstances?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17
utterances.text: Very often. When we were seeing battalion commanders and when visiting the lines, so you could say on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, did you have the impression that the men respected these orders in the course of combat; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17
utterances.text: I am sure that they respected these orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. I am going to move on to another subject. I would like to briefly go back to the issue of mortars. I think that you yourself had to, and this is a question I am putting to you, I think that you yourself assisted or were present when there was shelling; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17
utterances.text: When they shelled us, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, what -- I withdraw that. According to your personal experience, on the basis of your personal experience, can one hear the trajectory of a shell?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17
utterances.text: While it is coming it is impossible, but when it flies over you, when it is about to fall in the vicinity, then you hear a hissing or a sound similar to that. To be clearer, let's say if it falls about up to about 50 or 100 metres behind you, you then hear it as it is flying over you. At that moment you can hear it, if it is above you, in vertical terms. But the soldiers said that if you heard a shell, you wouldn't survive it because it would usually fall in your vicinity.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for your testimony and I am going to reread the transcript. You said that when it is arriving, it is not possible to hear it, and you meant to say you were referring to the shells trajectory before it hit its target; is that how I am to understand your testimony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. If we describe its trajectory as a parabola you can't hear it until it starts falling. I at least never had the opportunity of hearing the shell arriving. It is only when it starts falling you know how the parabola -- what the shape of the parabola is. When it starts falling, when it is in your vicinity, then you can hear it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: For the sake of time, could you always be as brief as possible. I would now like to ask you a certain number of questions with regard to the trenches. I will return to that in a minute, but there is just another question I have about weapons. You mentioned heavy weapons that the enemy side had. Could you tell us if you know anything about this how the enemy obtained his light weapons at the very beginning of the war, if you know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17
utterances.text: Well, he had obviously been preparing, he had prepared himself earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Could you expand on that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17
utterances.text: Well, he was preparing for war by using various trafficking channels. The enemy was arming himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17
utterances.text: Well, my knowledge relates to, and I'll give you the precise date, my first knowledge about weapons and lorries for Muslim was at the end of 1991. And then the second time I found out something about this was about the 10th of January 1992. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, I will interrupt you there. We will take this in order. You remember the end of 1991 and it appears the 10th of January 1992, can you tell us how you can remember this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17
utterances.text: On the 1st of March -- I have already mentioned that I saw Hungarian Kalashnikovs on the 1st of March at the barricades that the Muslims had put up near my flat in Alipasino Polje. That's when I personally saw them in the hands of these people. They were Hungarian Kalashnikovs and plastic butts that the JNA didn't produce, so these weren't from our sources. They -- the source was a Hungarian. It was produced in Hungary.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for this. Witness how can you know what happened at the end of 1991 and around the 10th of January 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17
utterances.text: At the entrance to the building in which I lived a lorry arrived one evening, a 3-ton Zastava lorry with Novi Pazar registration plates. And on that occasion in the evening hours, my friend and neighbour called me, his name was Boro Ivanisevic, he called me to tell me that I should look out since my flat was facing the other side of that building and in front of that building, he told me to have a look in front of the building. The Muslims were bringing weapons in. I had a look and I saw that they were taking out rifles. They were carrying them in bags. I couldn't make it out, but I could see who the producer of those weapons was. And as far as what I found out on the -- what I know about the 10th of January, my brother who worked in the ministry of interior, had told me that they had stopped a four-wheel drive which was being escorted by the MUP because it wasn't being escorted with an alarm light, and the policeman whose surname was Carmas said that it was suspicious. He stopped the vehicle and asked them what they were transporting and the reply was flour. But why is a police escort provided if flour is being transported and that gave him the idea -- he got the idea of lifting the tarpaulin. He had a look at the cases and he saw that there were rifles in the cases. He informed the police in Hadzici about that, that is also a municipality which is part of the town of Sarajevo, it is about 15 kilometres from the centre of the town to the south. Everyone turned up at the site. The chief, the secretary of the municipality, all the Muslims came and persuaded them to go to the station said that the vehicle would return. They waited in front of the station and the vehicle carried on, and later on it was sold, it was never found. So it went to the first Muslim villages which were not far from that place where the vehicle was stopped. And the third occasion I have already clarified that, those are the weapons that I saw in the hands of those who were manning the barricades on the 1st of March. That was all before the beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Before we move on to the question of civilians, I would like you to tell us something about the trenches. Were you in a position to see any trenches in the zone that was in a certain sense under your control?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17
utterances.text: You mean Muslim trenches? Yes, we saw such trenches.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you see them while they were being dug; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17
utterances.text: We saw them when they had already been dug, and while they were being dug.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know who carried out this work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17
utterances.text: Well, I know that for sure that mostly Serbian civilians were involved in this work in Sarajevo from the notorious Silos camp in Tarcin and from other Viktor Bubanj and from other private prisons around Sarajevo. They were forced to dig trenches, the Serbs were forced to do so. I know this for sure because I spoke to such people.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Were they shot at, I mean the people who were digging?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17
utterances.text: We never shot at people who weren't carrying rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. I would like to go back to the question of material damage, Witness. Could you tell us during which period property buildings were destroyed? When was the most extensive damage inflicted on buildings, during which period, could you tell us anything about that, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17
utterances.text: Well, it is difficult to give a precise time. One could refer to months. The most extensive damage was done in the period that started at the beginning of the war and up until mid-1993, in my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, I want to go back to the issue of fighting. When there was large-scale fighting between the two sides and I am referring to what you know on the Serbian side, obviously, was it possible for civilians to be wounded, not just soldiers but civilians too?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17
utterances.text: Well, of course. I remember that at the end of December, I remember an example that will illustrate what I want to say. I know that one mortar shell, 120-millimetre mortar shell which fell in the municipality, seven people were killed by this shell and 33 people were wounded. And I am not mistaken, another two succumbed to their wounds later on and many remained disabled, many people out of the 33 wounded remained disabled. That was towards the end of December 1992. Near the Blazuj hospital also, it is known that the hospital is was always just a civilian institution and my great friend Zeljko both his mother and father were killed at one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I am going to stop you here. Witness, do you have personal knowledge, even if it is approximate knowledge about the number of civilians injured from 1992 to 1994?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Objection, lack of foundation. No basis for asking this witness this type of question, Mr. President. It is also irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the question is to ask about the foundation as well, whether he has personal knowledge, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... several times that the Defence is asking whether someone has personal knowledge. I think the issue is what is the basis of that knowledge? And by just asking whether a witness has personal knowledge, that does not always give an answer to the question that is really involved, is that on what that personal knowledge is based. Could you -- you know that the -- the question has been put to you, Mr. DP17, whether you have any knowledge on the number of civilians injured from 1992 to 1994. And I -- Mr. Piletta-Zanin, perhaps the first clarification we would need to get an answer to that question is that what area? Is that the whole of Sarajevo or municipalities or the area where the witness was active? Do you have -- what did you have in mind when you asked the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Mr. President, of course we are speaking every time about one area. The Witness mentioned Blazuj hospital, so this is about the areas that the witness visited, I should have clarified this. I apologise. And of course we are also speaking about very specific areas that have to do with the brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In the area where your -- where you are fulfilling your duties, what would you know about the number of civilians, civilian casualties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know from the authorised organs in the Ilidza municipality that this is the period that you are speaking about that about 300 civilians were killed. And I know for sure that at the same time 460 soldiers were killed and 2.150 soldiers were injured during the war. I know this for certain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me then ask you: The authorised organs, who were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These were the organs that dealt with the -- these questions, because of course the civilian -- or the civilian authorities also functioned in the municipality of Ilidza like the registrar and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Who told you this? Let's -- before we talk about organs, talk about persons. Who told you the number of 300 civilian people killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Specifically I was told this by --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, perhaps there is a problem of possibility or necessity for closed session. Perhaps we could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We turn into closed session -- in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And would you then please answer the question. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This specific knowledge based on the analysis, medical certificates on the basis of the records that were kept by heads of personnel. Because chief of personnel there was such a person at the brigade command, because these people kept a record of everybody who was injured and the type of the injury. So they kept a record of people injured. I know that such a number for 1992 and 1993 was about 250 persons. I can't be quite sure whether it is 255, 256, but about 250 people killed in the Ilidza Brigade during 1992, 1993, that's how many there were. And as far as the entire war is concerned, there were 460 people killed, 2.250 [as interpreted] injured, which can tell you something about the fierceness of the fighting and the Muslim attacks that occurred during the war, the war that is the subject matter of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, counsel, please. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am sorry. On page 80, I am looking at another screen and it is line 10, and, yes, indeed it is a different number, I believe, that the one that we can see here. We were speaking about the injured because the French interpreter just told me that this is about 2.250 persons -- 2.150, this is what should appear now. Here it is. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, I am going to ask you some other questions in relation to a strategic target in the city of Sarajevo. You spoke to us about these persons who were leaving the city and were giving you information. First question: These people, were they able to leave the city throughout this period that we are interested in from September 1992 to August 1994; yes or no, if you can answer as much as you can?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, these persons, were they able to give you information of the strategic type; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17
utterances.text: Not all of them. Some of them were able to.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Those who were able to, what were these pieces of information, what was the type of information that they were able to provide?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17
utterances.text: Most of the time what we were interested in since the period has passed, we can speak about this, we were interested about the positions of mortars, tanks, field guns, where are their troops massing, where are their accommodation of their troops, are they preparing attacks, do they have -- if they had any information in relation to that. These were mostly the questions that we asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now speaking about the strictly military aspect about the weapons, was there also any aspect in terms of manufacturing weapons? Were you also interested in that, about the weapons industry?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Hypothetically speaking, did you get any specific information from these people speaking about this second aspect of the information?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us -- this Chamber something about this.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17
utterances.text: The knowledge, our knowledge, we knew that they were producing grenades, grenade launchers in the schools, Jaroslav Crni in the secondary technical engineering school, in the Vasin Miskin school, at the faculty of engineering, at the company called Zica. This is the information that I obtained during these interviews and gathering of information. This is what I can think of at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Very briefly, for the two schools that you mentioned and for the three other facilities, can you please give us their locations, if you can, the exact streets of the aforementioned, perhaps at least the neighbourhoods.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17
utterances.text: I know the neighbourhoods precisely. For most of them I know the streets as well, Jaroslav Crni school is near the Miljacka River, it is the so-called alley or the promenade. Then the engineering school is located at Marijn Dvor, that is the building next to the Holiday Inn Hotel. The company called Vasin Miskin Crni, that is what it was called before the war, this company is located next to the street Vojvoda Putnik [phoen] Street near the company for social protection, and then there is a school which I had the information about, and next to this Vasin Miskin school, this is where the shells and the grenade launchers were produced. I didn't have this information. I remembered it later on. And then in the Zica company across the bridge, the closest location to that company where the warehouse was, warehouse for tram vehicles, that was on the Alipasin Most, where the company was, and of course the faculty of engineering which was located at Kosevo. That would be the closest location, the closest reference point. That's what it would be. So that belonged to the municipality of Centar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, if I may just interrupt for one second. When we stop at 7.00 the Defence would have used two hours and 50 minutes, approximately. So if you say, well, we are more or less sticking to our estimate of time we would need, perhaps you could see whether you could finish by 7.00. If not, then, of course, we will have another 10 minutes tomorrow morning. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I am almost certain that I will manage to finish tonight. Thank you very much. May I proceed? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, thank you for listing these facilities. You spoke about the weapons that you were trying to locate or the positions, enemy positions that you tried to locate in the city. And I am talking about the mortars. These mortars, were they fixed, were they in one position, were they mobile, were they semi-mobile? What can you tell us about this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17
utterances.text: Most of the time they were mobile because there was this logic applied that you should never fire for a long time from one position, although there were also such that practically throughout the war they fired according to our information from one location, whether it was 500 metres to the right or to the left. And then they would fire again. But in any case, there were also fixed. So the answer would be there were fixed and there were mobile ones that would change location, but I have to say that we also had the information that they also had light mortars. These are 60-millimetre mortars on freight lorries that were moved throughout the city. So it was very hard to -- it was very difficult to find the exact location, the exact position that they were active from. It was hard to trace them, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I will interrupt you. Thank you very much. Where do you have this information from? You say we received the information, but how did you receive that information? Who provided this information to you at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17
utterances.text: From the persons who left the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, you spoke about lorries in plural. Did you know several cases, testimonies that mentioned such lorries; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17
utterances.text: Well, again, I say six years have passed. So I know they have spoken about this but it is hard to say whether it was one lorry or whether that one lorry appeared in several locations. But in any case, this information has been checked or has been corroborated by several people because people left, and it was about mortars active from the back of lorries.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Would it be possible to give us the names of the people that you have questioned on this subject; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17
utterances.text: It would be possible, but considering everything --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... private session for that reason, we will now turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, I can see that you are still thinking about that name. Please forget it. Just focus on the questions, please. The positions that were positions of your brigade, was it possible to see, for instance, cultural or religious facilities on the other side of the separation line; yes or no? I am talking about museums, mosques and so on.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17
utterances.text: The museums could not be seen. That's mostly newly built areas, and mosques dominated in the -- in the older part of town.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. But could you see them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17
utterances.text: No, unless I am very mistaken and if I can recall it correctly. See I cannot say for sure that there was a mosque in Hrasnica, although I have been to Hrasnica a hundred times, but I know there was a mosque in Butmir as far as these facilities were concerned, yes, you could see them. But as far as museums, theatres, cinemas, they were not in that part of town that bordered us, that would be my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. But theoretically speaking, would you be able to target or hit a cinema or a theatre, I mean hit with direct or indirect fire, would you theoretically speaking to hit such a facility?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17
utterances.text: No, no, because in Ilidza the cinema and the cultural centre hall, our troops held that. So these kind of halls, they were not outside of the area where we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, I am now speaking about the mosque that was located according to your testimony in Butmir. This mosque, was it, yes or no, at a distance that was within the range of a mortar; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Witness, do you know if this mosque that you told us about, was it ever attacked, fired on by your troops; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17
utterances.text: I didn't see it personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Witness, do you know about other facilities, cultural facilities, museums, theatres, cinemas or monuments that may have been within range looking from the positions that you had the control of?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the Serb booth, I am speaking about the positions, not certainly the weapons, but that will do. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Whether something is within the range, is that what you mean by that question? Is that your question? Well, yes, it was within the range, yes it was certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ever hit or did you ever attack fire on with your weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17
utterances.text: There was never such an order and I don't know that such facilities were attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. One last question, Witness, about light weapons. You spoke about that incident at the end of 1991 and the incident around the 10th of January 1992 and the incident in March when you spoke to us about. Now, I would like to go chronologically at the very beginning of the events which is more specifically the period when the JNA left Sarajevo as such. Can you tell us if you know when was that period when the JNA was leaving or left Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17
utterances.text: Well, the JNA --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Do you know that; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17
utterances.text: Approximately, yes, which means roughly speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. When the JNA was leaving Sarajevo, when it was withdrawing from Sarajevo in the part which would be -- which will be under the control of the enemy forces, do you know what happened with the weapons that may have been left in the barracks in that part, do you know; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17
utterances.text: Yes, I do know what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. What -- can you tell us what happened briefly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17
utterances.text: The Muslims took over the weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: And if you know, on the basis of what, what is the source of your knowledge? What is the origin of your knowledge? What and if you know what kind of weapons could these forces have at their disposal; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP17
utterances.text: Well, the forces managed to obtain not only infantry weapons, but also heavy weapons. Field guns, mortars, and tanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am finished, Mr. President, but I would just like to say that the English booth may have forgotten the heavy machine-gun at the very beginning when he listed the weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask for the transcript that special attention will be paid to page 87, especially where a question mark appears because I do not read in the transcript part of what in my recollection what I think I've heard. Mr. DP17, this concludes your examination by counsel for the Defence. I'd like to instruct you not to speak with anyone, not with the Prosecution, not with the Defence, not with anyone about your testimony that you have given in this court, and that you are about to give in this court. Tomorrow we will continue. You will then be further examined. We will adjourn until tomorrow morning -- tomorrow in the afternoon quarter past 2.00 in this same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, for the transcript, I just wanted to say something. Page 45, line 11, there was an overlapping of the questions of the Defence and the answers of the witness so I thought if perhaps those who are assisting us would pay special attention to this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Page 45, that is on your computer or on the other one. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I made sure that I copied it on the real transcript, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it then special attention will be paid to that. We will adjourn until tomorrow morning -- until tomorrow afternoon, I always make the same mistake. We will adjourn until a quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 7.05 p.m., to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 4th day of December, 2002, at 2.15 p.m.
